concept_html:
The DAMA-DMBOK (Data Management Body of Knowledge, second edition, revised in 2024) gives data teams a shared map. It splits data management into eleven knowledge areas, drawn as a wheel.

Data governance sits at the hub. It decides and oversees how the other ten are run. DMBOK2 defines it as the exercise of authority, control and shared decision-making (planning, monitoring and enforcement) over the management of data assets.

The ten spokes, with a talent example for each:

Knowledge area Talent example
Data architecture Bronze, silver and gold layers for HR data
Data modelling and design The person, position and organisation entities
Data storage and operations Lakehouse tables, backups, retention jobs
Data security Masking salary and health fields
Data integration and interoperability Feeds from the HR system and the learning platform
Document and content management Contracts, review forms, scanned certificates
Reference and master data One golden record per person, job codes, grades
Data warehousing and business intelligence Headcount and attrition reports
Metadata management Glossary entries, lineage, owners
Data quality Rules for missing managers or duplicate employee IDs

Two pairs get confused. Reference data is a controlled list of codes, such as grades or country codes. Master data is the agreed record of a core entity, such as the person. Metadata describes data: definitions, owners, lineage. Master data is the data itself.

The wheel is a checklist, not an org chart. A talent platform touches all eleven areas. When something breaks, name the area first, then the owner. A duplicate employee is a master data problem, not a reporting bug.

lines: - issue: headcount differs from payroll by 312
knowledge_area: reference and master data
root_cause: re-hired contractors get a second employee ID
owner: people master data owner
fix: match rule on national insurance number and date of birth, then merge

title: The DAMA wheel, eleven knowledge areas around governance
why_html: A firm's headcount report disagreed with payroll by 312 people. The BI team spent six weeks tuning report filters. The cause was in master data: contractors re-hired through an agency got a second employee ID, and nothing matched them to their first record. Naming the knowledge area on day one would have sent the problem to the master data owner.
